question.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}+3y={u}_{1}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-2}\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{1}(t)=u(t-1)$ is the unit step function.

$Y(s)=$
{{field-1}},$\,s>2$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}+3y\} & =L\{{u}_{1}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-2}\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}+3L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{1}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-2}\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0:$

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
{u}_{1}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-2}
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=1$ and $f(t)={e}^{2t-2}.$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed exponential forcing. 

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-1)\cdot {e}^{2t-2}\} & ={e}^{-s}\cdot L\{{e}^{2(t+1)-2}\} \\  & ={e}^{-s}\cdot L\{{e}^{2t}\} \\  & ={e}^{-s}\cdot \frac{1}{s-2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}\}+3L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{1}(t)\cdot {e}^{2t-2}\} \\ sY(s)+3Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s-2} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s-2} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{(s-2)(s+3)}\end{aligned}
$$
